reference.source: Williams Obstetrics / Novak's Gynecology / Campbell-Walsh Urology
clinicalPearls: Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome is a chronic condition of bladder or pelvic pain perceived to relate to the bladder, accompanied by urinary urgency and frequency, in the absence of infection or other identifiable cause
Pain characteristically worsens as the bladder fills and is relieved by voiding, a pattern that helps distinguish it from overactive bladder
It is far more common in women and frequently coexists with other chronic pain and functional conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome, fibromyalgia, and chronic pelvic pain
Diagnosis is essentially clinical and one of exclusion, requiring that infection, malignancy, stones, and other bladder pathology be ruled out
Cystoscopy may be normal or may reveal Hunner lesions, whose presence defines a distinct phenotype that responds to lesion-directed treatment
Management is stepwise, beginning with education, dietary trigger avoidance, stress and pain management, and pelvic floor physical therapy
Oral and intravesical therapies form later steps, and Hunner lesions are specifically treated by fulguration or resection
Refractory disease may be considered for neuromodulation or, rarely, major reconstructive surgery, reserved for carefully selected severe cases
New haematuria, especially in older patients or smokers, must trigger evaluation for bladder cancer rather than being ascribed to the syndrome
reference.pathophysiology: The mechanism is incompletely understood and probably multifactorial. A leading hypothesis is a defective bladder urothelial glycosaminoglycan (GAG) layer, which normally protects the underlying tissue; increased permeability allows urinary solutes such as potassium to penetrate the urothelium and irritate sensory nerves and detrusor muscle. Mast cell activation, neurogenic inflammation, and up-regulation of sensory pathways contribute to chronic pain and central sensitisation. In the Hunner lesion subtype there is a demonstrable inflammatory bladder wall change, whereas non-lesion disease is dominated by neuropathic and functional pain mechanisms, explaining the frequent overlap with other chronic pain disorders.
additionalDifferentials: Bladder carcinoma, including carcinoma in situ
Endometriosis and other gynaecological pelvic pain
Chronic prostatitis / chronic pelvic pain syndrome in men
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis and urine culture to exclude infection
Urine cytology and cystoscopy where malignancy is a concern, particularly with haematuria
Bladder diary documenting frequency, voided volumes, and symptom pattern
Validated symptom and pain questionnaires to assess severity and monitor response
Cystoscopy, with or without hydrodistension, to identify Hunner lesions
Imaging to exclude stones or other structural pathology when indicated
redFlags: Visible or microscopic haematuria requiring exclusion of bladder cancer
New or changing symptoms in an older patient or smoker
Persistent sterile pyuria warranting exclusion of tuberculosis or malignancy
Rapidly worsening or atypical pain suggesting an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The condition is chronic and typically follows a relapsing and remitting course; it is rarely progressive but can significantly impair quality of life. Many patients gain meaningful symptom control with a multimodal, stepwise approach, and the Hunner lesion subtype often responds well to lesion-directed therapy. A minority with severe refractory disease may ultimately require advanced interventions.
pitfalls: Repeatedly treating for infection despite negative cultures
Missing bladder cancer by attributing haematuria to the syndrome
Failing to identify and treat Hunner lesions, which need specific therapy
Escalating to invasive surgery before conservative and behavioural measures are exhausted
Overlooking coexisting pelvic floor dysfunction and other chronic pain conditions
management: Begin with conservative care: patient education, dietary trigger avoidance, fluid and stress management and bladder training
Refer for pelvic floor physical therapy directed at associated myofascial dysfunction, avoiding pelvic floor strengthening
Offer oral therapy such as amitriptyline, an antihistamine (hydroxyzine) or pentosan polysulfate alongside multimodal pain management
Escalate to intravesical instillations such as dimethyl sulfoxide, heparin or local anaesthetic for persistent symptoms
Perform cystoscopy with hydrodistension and treat Hunner lesions with fulguration, resection or intralesional corticosteroid
Reserve sacral neuromodulation and, in refractory disease, reconstructive surgery such as augmentation cystoplasty or urinary diversion
Manage flares and coexisting irritable bowel syndrome, fibromyalgia and chronic pelvic pain with multidisciplinary input
